How this text is transmitted

A short text in two layers: a 'classic' section attributed to Confucius and a commentary section attributed to his disciple Zengzi.

Also a chapter of the Lǐjì, promoted to one of the Four Books by Zhu Xi. The split between classic and commentary is a traditional attribution rather than a manuscript fact, and it is what makes the text's structure — eight items of cultivation in sequence — so teachable.

Reading caution. The text is a programme, not a collection of remarks: 'investigating things', 'extending knowledge', 'making the will sincere' and the rest are stages in one sequence running from the self outward to the empire. A single stage quoted alone loses the direction of the argument.

About this citation

A chapter of the Liji raised to independent canonical status by Zhu Xi in the twelfth century. The corpus cites it both as 'Liji, The Great Learning' and under its own title; those are one text, and the split between the classic section and Zengzi's commentary is a traditional attribution rather than a manuscript fact.

Reading the cited source

The archive attributes this English wording to The Great Learning and files it under Confucianism.

What a locator tells you, and what it does not · How this archive traces a quotation

About The Great Learning

The Dàxué is the shortest of the Four Books and the most programmatic. Like the Zhōngyōng it was lifted out of the Lǐjì by Zhu Xi, and it is traditionally divided into a brief 'classic' section attributed to Confucius and a commentary attributed to his disciple Zengzi.

Interpretation

The Great Learning uses the root-and-branch image to make a claim about order of dependence. Affairs have a sequence, and attending to what comes later without securing what comes earlier produces effort that cannot succeed. The claim is therefore about priority rather than importance: both root and branch matter, but they do not matter at the same time. Knowing which is which counts as being near the Way.

Why it matters

It supplies the question missing from most plans: what has to be true first? Getting the sequence wrong wastes work that is otherwise correct.

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “Things have roots and branches; affairs have ends…”?

“Things have roots and branches; affairs have ends…” comes from The Great Learning (Daxue) (Warring States period, c. 4th–3rd century BCE), attributed to The Great Learning.

What does The Great Learning mean by order?

Philosophers ask whether order is discovered in nature, imposed by rulers, or cultivated through custom. Chaos and creativity stand as its counterparts. This passage enters that discussion through order.
